content: In accordance with applicable laws, the waiver of informed consent is considered rare and exceptional. Such waivers must always receive approval from an ethical review committee. Guideline 5: Obtaining Informed Consent Essential Information for Prospective Research Subjects Before seeking an individual’s consent to participate in research, the investigator must provide the following information in a manner that the individual can understand: 1. The individual is being invited to participate in research, the reasons for their suitability, and that participation is entirely voluntary. 2. The individual has the right to refuse participation or withdraw at any time without penalty or loss of benefits they are otherwise entitled to. 3. The purpose of the research, the procedures involved, and how the research differs from routine medical care. 4. If applicable, details about randomization or blinding (e.g., double-blinding), and that the subject will not know their assigned treatment until the study concludes. 5. The expected duration of participation, including the number and length of visits to the research center, total time involved, and the possibility of early termination of the trial or their participation. 6. Whether monetary or material compensation will be provided for participation, and if so, the type and amount. 7. After the study concludes, subjects will be informed of the general findings and any results relevant to their health. 8. 9. Any foreseeable risks, pain, discomfort, or inconvenience to the individual or others, including risks to the health or well-being of a spouse or partner. 10. Any direct benefits expected from participation. 11. The anticipated benefits of the research to the community, society, or scientific knowledge. 12. Whether and how any proven safe and effective interventions or products will be made available to participants after the study, and whether they will need to pay for them. 13. Any currently available alternative treatments or interventions. 14. 15. The limits to the investigator’s ability to safeguard confidentiality and the potential consequences of breaches. 16. Assurance that no data will be shared with third parties (e.g., insurance companies or employers) without the subject’s consent. 17. Information about the research sponsors, the investigators’ institutional affiliations, and the sources of funding. 18. Possible research uses of the subject’s medical records and biological specimens collected during clinical care. 19. Whether biological specimens will be destroyed after the research concludes, and if not, details about their storage, future use, and the subject’s right to refuse storage or request destruction. 20. Whether commercial products may be developed from biological specimens and whether participants will receive any benefits from such developments. 21. Whether the investigator is acting solely as a researcher or also as the subject’s physician. 22. The extent of the investigator’s responsibility to provide medical care to participants. 23. That treatment for research-related injuries or complications will be provided free of charge, including details about the nature, duration, and funding of such care. 24. How compensation for disability or death resulting from research-related injuries will be provided, if applicable. 25. Whether the right to compensation is legally guaranteed in the country where the research is conducted. 26. Confirmation that the research protocol has been approved by an ethical review committee. Guideline 6: Obligations of Sponsors and Investigators in Obtaining Informed Consent Sponsors and investigators must: Avoid unjustified deception, undue influence, or intimidation. Obtain signed informed consent from each subject, unless exceptions are justified and approved by an ethical review committee. Renew informed consent if significant changes occur in the research conditions or procedures, or if new information arises that could affect the subject’s willingness to continue. Renew informed consent at predetermined intervals in long-term studies, even if no changes occur in the research design or objectives. Guideline 7: Inducement to Participate Subjects may be reimbursed for lost earnings, travel costs, and other expenses incurred during participation. They may also receive free medical services. Compensation for inconvenience and time spent is permissible, especially for those receiving no direct benefit from the research. However, payments or services must not be so excessive as to unduly influence subjects to participate against their better judgment. All compensation must be approved by an ethical review committee. Guideline 8: Interventions offering direct diagnostic, therapeutic, or preventive benefits must be justified by their expected advantages compared to available alternatives, considering foreseeable risks and benefits. Risks of interventions without direct benefits must be justified by the expected societal benefits, such as generalizable knowledge. These risks must be reasonable in relation to the importance of the knowledge to be gained. Guideline 9: Special Limitations on Risk for Individuals Unable to Provide Informed Consent When research involves individuals incapable of giving informed consent, the risks of interventions without direct benefits must not exceed those of routine medical or psychological examinations. Slight increases in risk may be permitted if there is a compelling scientific or medical rationale and approval from an ethical review committee. Guideline 10: The research addresses the health needs and priorities of the population. Any interventions, products, or knowledge generated will be made reasonably available to benefit the population. Guideline 11: Choice of Control in Clinical Trials As a general rule, control group participants should receive an established effective intervention. In certain circumstances, alternative comparators such as placebos may be ethically acceptable, provided they do not expose subjects to serious or irreversible harm. Guideline 12: Exclusion of groups that might benefit from participation must be justified. Guideline 13: Research Involving Vulnerable Persons Special justification is required for involving vulnerable individuals in research. Guideline 14: The research cannot be equally well conducted with adults. The research aims to address health needs relevant to children. Parental or legal guardian permission is obtained. The child’s assent is obtained to the extent of their capability. A child’s refusal to participate or continue in the research is respected. Guideline 15: The research cannot be conducted with individuals capable of providing informed consent. The research addresses health needs specific to this population. Consent is obtained to the extent of the individual’s capability, and their refusal is respected unless exceptional circumstances apply. Permission is obtained from a responsible family member or legally authorized representative. Guideline 16: Women as Research Subjects Women of reproductive age should not be excluded from biomedical research solely due to the potential for pregnancy. However, risks to the woman and fetus must be thoroughly discussed, and access to pregnancy testing and effective contraception must be provided before research begins. Guideline 17: Pregnant Women as Research Participants Pregnant women should be presumed eligible for biomedical research participation. Research in this population should address specific health needs and be supported by reliable evidence, particularly regarding teratogenic and mutagenic risks. Guideline 18: Subjects must be informed of any limitations to confidentiality and the potential consequences of breaches. Guideline 19: Right of Injured Subjects to Treatment and Compensation Subjects injured as a result of research participation are entitled to free medical treatment and equitable compensation for any resulting impairment or disability. In the case of death, their dependents are entitled to compensation. Subjects must not be asked to waive their right to compensation. Guideline 20: Strengthening Capacity for Ethical and Scientific Review Sponsors and investigators in externally sponsored research have an ethical obligation to contribute to the capacity of resource-limited countries to design, conduct, and review biomedical research. Capacity-building activities may include establishing ethical review committees, strengthening research infrastructure, and training healthcare and research staff. Guideline 21: Essential health-care services for the safe conduct of research. Treatment for research-related injuries. Services necessary to make beneficial interventions or products developed through research reasonably available to the population or community concerned.
